name: Storage persistence and eviction
plain: A site can ask the browser to keep its data permanently; otherwise it can be evicted when disk is low.
meaning: navigator.storage.persist() asks for protected storage. Chrome grants it from engagement, bookmarks or install, Firefox asks the person. Best effort data is deleted least recently used first. storage.estimate() reveals quota, a coarse signal.

access.prompt_ui: Firefox shows a permission prompt, Chrome decides silently
access.persistence: Persistent until cleared by the person. Best effort until eviction
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can ask the browser to keep its saved data when space runs low
limits.user_action: Firefox may ask you to allow Store data in persistent storage. Other browsers decide quietly.
can: Check how much space it has used and has left, roughly
cannot: Stop you clearing site data yourself
Keep data after a private window closes
limits.differs: Firefox asks you. Chrome decides on its own. Safari decides on its own and supports it only in part.

story.what_it_is: A site can ask the browser to keep its data for good. Otherwise low disk space can erase it.

marketing.name: Persistent storage
marketing.pitch: Google explains how a site can ask the browser to protect its data from automatic cleanup.

marketing.name: Updates to storage policy
marketing.pitch: Apple explains how Safari handles storage limits and when it can clear a site's data.

story.for_you: Most of the time nothing seems to happen. But if your device runs low on space, a site you rarely use may lose its offline data and ask you to log in or download again.
story.for_makers: Makers want their data to survive, because a lost offline copy means a frustrated user. They request protection, and browsers grant it based on use. Trackers also like data that outlives clearing.

use_cases.example: A browser game asks to protect your saves so a low disk does not erase your progress.
A note app asks to protect offline notes that are not yet synced to the cloud.
A web editor asks to protect a long project saved only on your device.
A podcast or music app asks to keep your downloads.
A browser clears old data first from sites you rarely visit, to free up space.
A tracker hides an ID in storage that the browser might never clear on its own.

technical_bounds: Chrome decides persist by heuristics with no prompt
estimate() values are padded or rounded to resist fingerprinting
Safari applies the 7 day cap except for installed web apps

abuse: Ensuring tracker storage is not evicted
